clue.text: Flexible on detail needed to make calls  …

definitions.note: describes the answer: a dial tone is the thing needed before you can make calls

indicators.note: letters that are flexible can bend into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone willing to bend on the small print in order to get a deal done, the dots running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this clue to 2 down as one sentence; each still works alone. 'Flexible on detail' reads as a trait of character, not an instruction to rearrange ON DETAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A dial tone is the hum a landline gives when it is ready, and you need it before you can place a call.

clue.text: …  essential to game show for network

indicators.note: what is essential to something sits at its core, so the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 down: a quality a television game show needs before a network will take it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Network' in the surface is a TV channel; as the definition it is a net of crossing threads.
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh is a network of interlaced wires or threads.

clue.text: Device providing broad with good time

blocks.note: t = time, as in physics formulas

explanation.surface: A gadget that promises a woman a good time, 'broad' being old American slang for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: G goes inside WIDE, between the D and the E, and T is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A widget is any small gadget or mechanical device.

clue.text: Intimidate dodgy spy with subtle touch

indicators.note: something dodgy is not straight, so SPY comes out rearranged
a subtle touch works by indirection, so TOUCH is rearranged

explanation.surface: A shady agent frightens someone with a delicate hint rather than an open threat.
explanation.walkthrough: Each anagram indicator governs only the word right after it, so the clue gives two short anagrams in a row rather than one long one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: undermining an opponent's confidence with mind games intimidates them, as a boxer might at the weigh-in.

clue.text: Notices unwelcome sign

blocks.note: surface: a verb, someone spotting something; setter: a plural noun, printed notices such as flyers and leaflets
surface: a bad omen; setter: a sticker on a door telling leafleters their notices are unwelcome

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'notices' as a verb and the clue is about spotting a bad omen; read it as a plural noun and it is a sign on a letterbox saying leaflets are unwelcome.
explanation.definitionFit: A NO JUNK MAIL sticker on a door is a sign saying that advertising notices are unwelcome.

clue.text: It makes you an ugly little man when injecting drug

blocks.note: a gnome is a small ugly man of folklore

explanation.surface: A warning that injecting drugs will turn you into a shrivelled little man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It makes you' looks like the start of a threat; it is the whole definition, since your genome is what makes you who you are.
explanation.definitionFit: A genome is an organism's full set of genes, the blueprint that makes you.

clue.text: Type of guarantee you can't pass on

definitions.text: Type of guarantee you can't pass on

blocks.note: a kind of warranty offered on goods, named for how long it lasts
surface: a warranty you cannot transfer to another owner; setter: the span in which you have not died, 'pass on' meaning die

explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't pass on' reads as 'can't transfer to someone else', as with many guarantees; it also means you haven't died, which is exactly what your lifetime is.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifetime guarantee lasts as long as you live, the span during which you have not passed on.

clue.text: Fantasy language may support second word for greedy

blocks.note: s = second, as in units of time

explanation.surface: A made-up tongue might supply a second, less blunt word for greed.
explanation.walkthrough: This works only because 8 is a down entry: put S on top of ELFISH and the column reads SELFISH, a word for greedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Elfish, or Elvish, is the invented language of the elves in Tolkien's fantasy novels.

clue.text: One curing lungs? Yes and (definitely) no

definitions.text: One curing lungs? Yes and (definitely) no

blocks.note: one who cures preserves food over wood fires, offal included
yes for the food-preserver; definitely no for the cigarette habit, which ruins lungs

explanation.walkthrough: A smoker cures meat or fish, including organs like lungs, by smoking them: 'yes'. A smoker of cigarettes is definitely not curing their own lungs: 'no'.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoker is both someone who cures food with smoke and someone whose habit harms the lungs.

clue.text: Dull talk starts by lecturing about heraldry

indicators.note: we keep the starts of the next four words

explanation.surface: A lecturer droning on about coats of arms is the very picture of dull talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The four words that supply the letters are themselves an example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Blah is empty, boring talk, as in 'blah blah blah'.

clue.text: Fit up goon caught forging voucher

indicators.note: forging hammers material into a new shape, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A thug framed and arrested for counterfeiting a voucher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit up' is British slang for framing someone, which makes the surface read as a crime story.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift coupon is a voucher given as a present, exchangeable for goods.

clue.text: It's revealing, as hooligan takes over facility

explanation.surface: A thug occupying a public building gives something away, the news revealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' is a polite word for a toilet, and the WC is the crossword's favourite one.
explanation.definitionFit: A low-cut top or dress shows a lot of the chest, so it is revealing.

clue.text: Ineptitude shown since slums demolished

indicators.note: demolished buildings are knocked down and their pieces scattered

explanation.surface: Bungling by the planners has been on display ever since the slums were torn down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Since' looks like a time word in the surface; it is simply half of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsiness is a lack of skill or deftness, which is ineptitude.

clue.text: Squatter in store that is rented initially

indicators.note: we keep only the initial letter of 'rented'

blocks.note: a store of goods is stock

explanation.surface: Someone living without permission in a shop, when the place is supposed to be let.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squatter' reads as a noun, someone occupying a building; it is the comparative adjective, more squat.
explanation.definitionFit: Squatter, meaning shorter and broader, means the same as stockier.

clue.text: Put back up and charged again at hearing

indicators.note: at a hearing, the words are listened to rather than read

blocks.note: charged again = rebilled, sent another bill; it is the sound we need

explanation.surface: Someone remanded and charged afresh at a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put back up' sounds like a prisoner returned to the dock, and 'hearing' like a court session.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebuild something is to put it back up after it has fallen or been knocked down.

clue.text: Singular audience for an extra difficult crossword

blocks.note: one member of an audience for radio or a talk
a weekly British puzzle famous as the hardest of them all

explanation.surface: A difficult puzzle aimed at a small, special kind of solver.
explanation.walkthrough: The Listener is a famously hard weekly crossword, now published in The Times, named after an old BBC magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: 'singular' makes the audience one person, a hearer; and the proper name of a notoriously hard thematic puzzle.

clue.text: Mate tips off significant fugitive

indicators.note: with both tips taken off MATE, only its middle letters stay

blocks.note: mATe, with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A friend informs on an important escaped criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips off' looks like informing on someone; it means cutting off the tips of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive is at large, still free and not yet caught.

clue.text: Men and girls make up the cause of mechanical problems

indicators.note: the letters are used to make up something new

explanation.surface: Boys and girls kiss and make up, and somehow that is why machines break down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make up' suggests a reconciliation in the surface; here the letters of MEN and GIRLS make up the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gremlins are the imaginary imps blamed for unexplained mechanical faults, a joke from RAF pilots.

clue.text: Fat fool starts failing test subject

indicators.note: the starts of both words fail, so each loses its first letter

explanation.surface: An overweight idiot flunking an exam in some school subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' is plural, so both FLAB and PRAT lose their first letters. 'Test subject' looks like an exam paper; it is an animal in an experiment.
explanation.definitionFit: A lab rat is an animal, or jokingly a person, used as the subject of experiments.

clue.text: A shire is unusual location for Douglas

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement of the letters is what we need

explanation.surface: A county is an odd place to find a man called Douglas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Douglas' looks like a person; it is the capital of the Isle of Man, which lies in the Irish Sea between Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas, on the Isle of Man, is located in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Losing oxygen, soldier returns to tell the tale

indicators.note: in a down entry, returning sends the letters back the other way

blocks.note: a trooper is a soldier, especially in the cavalry
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A soldier, short of breath, comes home to tell what happened.
explanation.walkthrough: TROOPER loses one of its two Os to give TROPER, which read backwards is REPORT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: telling the tale of what happened is giving an account of it, as a returning soldier would to his officer.

clue.text: It provides a seasonally crisp description when ready

definitions.text: It provides a seasonally crisp description when ready

blocks.clueFragment: It provides a seasonally crisp description
blocks.note: 'seasonally' means with seasoning; the crisp is a British potato crisp, and the answer is a word naming its flavour
the word completes a flavour name when it follows 'ready'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Seasonally' means with seasoning, not by time of year. Ready salted is the British name for plain salted potato crisps, what Americans call potato chips.
explanation.definitionFit: Following 'ready', SALTED completes the description of a crisp flavour that is seasoned only with salt.

clue.text: Santa set off before five; it keeps him on track

indicators.note: SANTA is set off, sent out of his usual shape

explanation.surface: Father Christmas sets out on his rounds before five, guided by a gadget that keeps him on course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' is Santa departing in the surface; in the wordplay it scrambles his name. Satnav is British for a GPS navigation device.
explanation.definitionFit: A satnav is a satellite navigation device, which keeps a driver on the right route.

clue.text: Respect one broadcasting what's already well known

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters the letters widely, like seed thrown out

explanation.surface: Praise for a broadcaster who reports only things everybody knows already.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcasting' looks like it belongs to the one on air; it tells us to scatter RESPECT ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: An open secret is supposedly confidential but actually already widely known.

clue.text: Spring double can be said to surprise

definitions.text: double can be said to surprise
definitions.note: WELL doubled, 'well, well', is what you say when surprised

blocks.note: a spring of water, not the season or a leap

blocks.clueFragment: double can be said to surprise
blocks.note: a word that, said twice over, is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: The second half describes the word rather than defining it: said twice, as 'well, well!', it expresses surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A well is a spring of water, and 'well, well' is an exclamation of surprise.

clue.text: One obsessed by subject that captured king

explanation.surface: A fanatic for a single topic who once took a king prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Captured king' reads as a chess move or a war story; it is WON then K.
explanation.definitionFit: A wonk is someone obsessively studious about one subject, like a policy wonk.

clue.text: Conservative philosopher sounds like he was isolated

indicators.note: we need a spelling that sounds like the philosopher's name

blocks.note: C = Conservative, the British political party

explanation.surface: A right-wing thinker whose public voice has made him a lonely outcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the philosopher's name is heard; C is added as spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe, in Defoe's novel, lived cast away alone on an island.

clue.text: Lagging behind, learner turns to north for instruction

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plates on British learner drivers' cars

explanation.surface: A slow pupil who has fallen behind heads north to get some teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: In TRAILING the L becomes N, giving TRAINING.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the instruction given to learners, which fits the learner already in the wordplay.
